值得閱讀的理由

  • 洞察高性價比模型策略：了解 MiniMax 如何在算力資源受限的環境下，以僅十分之一的推論成本實現全球頂尖模型 95% 的效能表現。
  • 拆解多模態與語言模型的整合趨勢：探討將語言與影音生成深度融合為單一模型的技術前瞻性，以及其如何重塑創意與影音製作產業的商業價值。
  • 理解後訓練時代的競爭優勢：藉由精闢的「高爾夫練習球」比喻，掌握為何推論成本是決定強化學習與規模化「後訓練」勝負的核心關鍵。

摘要

從算力狂熱到極致效能的突圍策略

作者指出，MiniMax 創辦人閆俊傑在近期訪談中透露，其模型表現已達到全球頂級模型的 95%，但推論成本僅為十分之一。閆俊傑早年經歷過百度時期最大規模的 GPU 集群研究，深知算力的力量，但在創立 MiniMax 後明確選擇不與美國實驗室硬碰硬比拼硬體規模，而是將核心聚焦於「榨取每顆 GPU 的最大價值」。面對國內外激烈的百模大戰，MiniMax 專注於高勝率的方向，深耕底層系統架構與訓練基礎設施，確保計算晶片能發揮極致運作效率。

以降低成本與科學突破重新定義 AGI

作者提及，MiniMax 的名稱本身就蘊含了「成本最小化、智慧最大化」的願景。閆俊傑對通用人工智慧（AGI）的定義並非僅止於聊天或撰寫文章，而是 AI 能否自主提出全新科學理論以推動人類科學前沿。在技術路徑上，團隊早期便鎖定多模態路線，歷經虛擬陪伴產品 Glow 的驗證與 GPT-4 帶來的時間表震撼，將技術體系收斂為專注生產力的 M 系列語言模型與可跨模態生成的 H 系列影音模型。

打破割裂：邁向全流程統一多模態模型

針對現有影音生成模型的局限，作者引述投資機構觀點指出，當前影音模型雖然畫面出色，卻缺乏理解複雜剪輯指令與創作意圖的能力；而語言模型理解反饋卻無法直接產出畫面。MiniMax 計劃在數月內將 M 系列與 H 系列合併為統一大型模型，這將使 AI 具備承接完整專案、理解細緻修改指令並自動執行的能力，讓未來的商業變現模式從「按秒計費」躍升為「按整體專案交付價值收費」。

低成本推論構築的後訓練飛輪

在商業與營運層面，作者說明 MiniMax 堅持利潤來自技術創新帶來的成本下降，而非調漲價格。針對當前的 AI 競爭格局，訪談中引用了極為生動的「高爾夫練習球比喻」：當今模型能力的躍升關鍵在於消化數據後的「後訓練（Post-training）」，每一次任務嘗試與回饋調整都需要調用推論。如果擁有全球最便宜的練習球（低推論成本），就能以相同預算進行最高頻率的後訓練與強化學習，進而打造出世界上規模最大的後訓練系統，推動模型通往頂級智能。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. Our model's performance hits about 95%of the world's top models, yet the inference cost is only one-tenth of theirs. This is what MiniMax founder Yan Junjie recently said in a podcast interview. The host of this podcast is the veteran British investment trust Scottish Mortgage, which is also an institution that participated in MiniMax's funding. I listened to the entire podcast and read several Chinese analyses of it. My biggest takeaway wasn't the 95%and one-tenth figures themselves, but the entire logic of operation hidden behind these numbers. In the interview, Yan made it very clear : he doesn't want to compete with Americans on raw computing power. From day one, he knew that path wouldn't work in China, so he chose a completely different route. What route is that? It is to squeeze more useful output out of every single GPU; this approach is evident from his personal background. Yan Junjie was born in a small town in Henan. His father was a local math teacher. He began self-studying university-level math and computer science in middle school, and later entered the Institute of Automation at the Chinese Academy of Sciences for his graduate studies. About 20 years ago,. deep learning was still a very niche field, but he was already convinced that if you scaled the methods large enough, AI would inevitably become much more powerful. During his PhD, the AlexNet paper from the University of Toronto made a huge impact on him. That was in 2012, when deep learning significantly outperformed traditional methods in image classification for the first time . He made a direct decision then: join the company with the most GPUs. In 2014 , Baidu was his top choice, as it possessed the world's largest GPU cluster. The research atmosphere was very open when he joined. As an intern,. during peak periods, he could single-handedly mobilize one-third of Baidu's GPUs. He used this computing power for image classification and object detection research, and partnered with another intern to enter the ImageNet competition, where they took third place globally. That was the first time he personally experienced how computing power could change the speed of research. Later, he joined SenseTime for over six years, rising to become Vice President and Deputy Dean of the Research Institute. At the end of 2021, he left SenseTime to found MiniMax. When the company was established, GPT had not yet been released. He knew Artificial General Intelligence was important, but he wasn't sure how long it would take.

During its first year, MiniMax focused primarily on building infrastructure to train language models, image generation models, and audio generation models. To test the effectiveness of their models, they also created a virtual companion product called Glow. As a result, the user base grew very quickly; what was originally just an experimental product ended up attracting millions of users. Four months later, OpenAI released GPT- 4. Yan said in an interview that GPT-4 completely changed their judgment on the timeline. He had originally thought the pace of AI scaling would be much slower , but now it seems that's not the case, and they must accelerate everything immediately. MiniMax began to increase. computing facilities, expand data, and make their models larger. At the same time, competition emerged all of a sudden; before the release of ChatGPT, there were very few startups in China seriously working on large models, but shortly after, about 20 companies appeared, plus giants like ByteDance, Alibaba, and Baidu with their own plans , suddenly crowding MiniMax onto a much more packed table. So the question became very realistic: with less computing power than the competition, can they still remain on the frontier? The answer Yan Junjie gave is very simple: efficiency. Top-tier US laboratories can run dozens of technical. routes simultaneously and pick the one that performs the best. MiniMax doesn't have that many GPUs; he mentioned the company currently has about 500 employees. Compared to well-funded US labs, MiniMax must focus its energy on directions with higher probabilities of success; they cannot afford to experiment blindly. Therefore, they have invested heavily in model architecture and training infrastructure for the long term. These efforts won't immediately turn into a new product, but once the training scale grows, model scheduling, data processing, and GPU utilization all rely on these underlying systems to hold things up. If the infrastructure is not built well, even newly purchased chips might sit idle for part of the time. He. did one thing quite early on: he baked the company's direction right into its name, "MiniMax"—minimizing cost and maximizing intelligence, meaning to push inference costs to the lowest and intelligence levels to the highest. Yan said in a podcast that before large models and AGI became mainstream concepts, MiniMax was already China's first domestic AGI company. So, what is MiniMax's definition of AGI? He said it's not about being able to chat or write articles, but about AI being able to autonomously propose new scientific theories. Future major scientific breakthroughs will mainly rely on AI. So , whether it can push the scientific.

frontier is the standard by which he judges AGI. In terms of product layout, MiniMax chose the multimodal route from the start; this decision was later proven to be forward-looking, though at the time it was actually a bit out of necessity, because early in the company's founding, they weren't sure what form the final AI would take, so they expanded in every direction, waiting for the technology to mature before merging them. Now, their products have been integrated into two major model families. The first is the M-series language models, geared toward productivity scenarios like coding and AI agents; the second is the H-series video generation models, capable of. cross-modal processing of video, image, and audio. H3 is their flagship model, which is now open-source; it was the most downloaded open-weights model globally last month, with approximately 25 million downloads. He stated that these two series will not remain separate forever. The plan is to scale them individually first, then merge them into a unified large model in the coming months. Lawrence Burns, an investment manager at SOTIMG, specifically analyzed the value of this unified model in the latter half of the podcast. He said that current video models actually have limitations: they are good, but they. don't understand editing instructions. For example, if you tell it to "cut this middle part, change the ending, and make the color tone warmer," it can't do it yet. They are adept at generating clips from scratch but struggle to understand the intent and language behind the act of editing. This requires the comprehension capabilities of a language model. Conversely, the same applies: language models can understand an editor's feedback, but they cannot shoot video themselves. If MiniMax can deeply integrate the two, the boundaries of AI capabilities will shift; it will no longer just generate a five-second clip , but be able to handle a complete creative brief, a short film, or even a. design project, managing the entire process from understanding requirements to execution. Burns said that once AI reaches this stage, the money customers are willing to pay won't be calculated by the clip, but by the entire project. Regarding the business model, Yan Jing was very blunt: an AI company's profit doesn't come from price hikes, but from using technological innovation to drive down inference costs. Low inference cost is both their moat for generating revenue and their moat for realizing profit; this efficiency allows them to pursue an API-driven business model rather than relying on one-off transactions. Revenue growth has indeed.

been fast this year; as of August, ARR exceeded $ 800 million, with B2B business accounting for over 80%, though the company is still operating at a loss . Actual revenue for the first half of 2026 was $ 116.6 million, a year-on-year increase of over 300%, but the adjusted net loss was $ 93 million, roughly 2.5 to 3 times their revenue for the same period. R&D investment is increasing, and computing power procurement continues; in July 2025, they raised another $ 2 billion, specifically to keep pace with frontier models. Furthermore, the price war in the Chinese model market continues. DeepSeek. , Alibaba, and ByteDance all have their own models and products. Even after MiniMax cuts costs, they still face competitors lowering their prices, so Yan Junjie says revenue growth must outpace cost growth—that is the ideal path. Vince made a golf analogy that I think is particularly good. He says AI model training happens in two steps: the first is digesting massive data to gain knowledge, called pre-training; the second is post-training, where the model practices repeatedly, tries to do a task , checks if the result is good, and then adjusts. All the major leaps in models over the past two years, from writing code to executing tasks, have all come. from the post-training stage. And this practice process is very expensive, because every time the model practices, it must be called, and each call incurs an inference fee. Chain. To improve their level, if one person's practice balls are much cheaper , given the same budget, they can buy more balls and practice more, naturally progressing faster. MiniMax wants to be the one with the cheap practice balls. Low inference costs not only allow for cheaper APIs but also let the model conduct more post-training sessions itself. Since reinforcement learning and data synthesis in post-training rely on. inference, cheaper inference means larger-scale post-training. Junjie says that at some point in the future, MiniMax might be able to build the world's largest post-training system, which could lead to frontier intelligence. Open-source is another unique choice for MiniMax. US companies like OpenAI and Anthropic keep their models closed, charging users for access while withholding the weights, so users cannot run them on their own devices. MiniMax opened its model weights. Just two weeks after the release of Hailuo-3 , about 300 derivative open models were created, one of the more well-known being "H3Max" from the US company A-H 3 . Building on Hailuo-3, they performed.

rapid post-training to generate five seconds of video in three seconds, turning it into a real-time video generator. Once the speed is up, some brand-new use cases emerge. For example , developers have already set up 24/7 uninterrupted AI live streams, with video content generated in real-time based on audience input. Vince says the imaginative potential for this real-time video is massive. Real-time gaming, interactive education, and live commerce —things that were impossible before are now possible. Open-source has another layer of benefits: corporate and government clients can deploy and host models themselves, without needing to send data to MiniMax, making privacy and. security easier to control. Over the past six months, the issue of AI sovereignty has become increasingly critical. If your business is built on a centralized model, can you really count on continued access in the long run? What exactly will happen to your data? These concerns have given open-source models a natural advantage. Yan Yunjie says that open source is not the opposite of commercialization, but a catalyst for it and for continuous innovation; it’s a triple win for model vendors, end users, and developers. The plan is to remain committed to open source until AGI is achieved. The core goal is to deliver 95%of the performance at 1%of the cost. Yan Yunjie cautions. that what truly matters is not the gap at a specific point in time, but the speed of model iteration, as both China and the U.S. are still in the very early stages on the road to AGI. He notes that this final 5%gap may be even harder to bridge than the initial 95%progress. So , closing the current gap may take more time; over the past three years, the pace of progress between U.S. and Chinese models has been roughly comparable, and he focuses on iteration rates rather than leaderboard rankings. Regarding the issue of compute constraints, he says this is something Chinese AI companies must face together , but it is precisely these constraints that have made them better engineers and. researchers. The more limited the compute, the more critical algorithmic innovation and inference optimization become. Many cutting-edge U.S. labs are somewhat spoiled by an abundance of compute, allowing them to explore the boundaries of model capabilities at scale without being forced to prioritize efficiency from day one like Chinese companies. Yan also says he designed the model architecture with the intent that it could maintain excellent performance regardless of the chip it runs on. When hardware is constrained, the value of model architecture, infrastructure, and low-level optimization is amplified many times over. Regarding the differences.

between the U.S. and Chinese AI ecosystems, Yan’s judgment is clear: they will not follow the same path. The U.S. ecosystem is using massive capital to support closed systems, while the Chinese ecosystem is using efficiency to support collaboration. U.S. companies have more compute, more funding, and easier access to chips, while Chinese companies are forced to maximize output efficiency per unit of compute. Open source versus closed, high efficiency versus resource abundance—these fundamental differences will breed different types of innovation. Why invest in 01.AI? Vince summarizes three reasons; the first is the 95% performance at 1%cost figure. And the culture of efficiency behind it. He says. when he first met Yan Yunjie in December 2025, he was very curious about what was happening in the Chinese AI ecosystem. He believes this low-cost model has value on a global scale. Not all jobs require the most advanced models, and not every user or company is as wealthy as those in the West, capable of bearing such high costs. Second is Yan Junjie himself; Burns says he rarely meets someone who is both a highly respected AI scientist and an excellent capital allocator. AI labs, especially those in the U.S., will pour massive amounts of money into running dozens of experimental paths at once to see which. one succeeds. But Yan's brilliance lies in his ability to successfully narrow the number of experiments, focus on fewer options, spend less money, and still achieve great results. Burns said he spoke with many in the Chinese AI circle who have worked with Yan for years, and everyone agrees his ability to predict tech trends is a core strength, while his reputation as a scientist helps him attract top-tier AI talent. In the field of AI, talent is just as scarce and expensive as computing power. Third is Burns 'basic assessment: AI is developing rapidly in both the U.S. and Chinese ecosystems, and it's hard to judge where AI is. heading if you only look at one place. In early 2026, they participated in the MiniMax IPO with an initial investment of about 20 million pounds. After the IPO, the stock performed well, and they have already cashed out 40 million pounds, effectively doubling their initial investment while still holding onto shares. He calls this a classic asymmetric bet. The market is large enough; as long as MiniMax succeeds in its mission, it won't lack buyers. However, competition and profitability are real challenges—price wars are intense, with giants like ByteDance cutting prices, and the cost of maintaining models is rising, with.

losses currently about three times the revenue. He says this is the normal state for early-stage investments: the outcome could be very good, but it is also highly uncertain, which is why MiniMax's weight in the entire portfolio won't be too large. Regarding organizational culture, Yan Junjie summarizes MiniMax's principles into two points: first, keep things simple; although there are multi-modal models, the underlying architecture and infrastructure remain very streamlined. Second, always build infrastructure. Refining infrastructure is sometimes more important than launching products quickly, as it is the foundation for scaling. Other traits, such as a flat. structure, efficiency, and focus, are simply the results of these two principles naturally evolving under constraints. Finally, when asked what the world will look like after MiniMax achieves its vision, Yan Junjie said the question isn't whether AI can achieve it , but who it will benefit. AI is so important that it shouldn't belong to any one company, country, or organization; it must belong to all of humanity. He said the company's mission statement is "Intelligence with everyone ," rather than "Intelligence for everyone," as if intelligence were something they provide to everyone. In. his view, AGI should belong to the model's users, the developers building applications on top of it, and the researchers contributing to it; together , they determine what kind of system the model ultimately becomes. Watching this interview, my biggest takeaway is that Yan Jing has shown us an AI expansion path that is completely different from the mainstream Silicon Valley model. The Silicon Valley story is about more compute, more money, and training larger models, while Max's story is about doing more efficient things with fewer resources. It is hard to say who will succeed on. this path, but one thing is certain: the global AI race is not just playing out in Silicon Valley. Do you think this efficiency-first approach taken by Chinese AI companies can eventually catch up to or even surpass them? Let me know in the comments.

本期节目解析MiniMax创始人闫俊杰接受英国投资信托Scottish Mortgage播客专访的完整内容，包含三位中文译稿遗漏的播客后半段投资复盘。面对算力与资本双重约束，闫俊杰选择了一条完全不同于硅谷的AI扩展路径——以极致推理效率为核心，将前沿模型成本压到头部竞品的1/10，同时保持约95%的性能。口播稿完整呈现了闫俊杰从河南小城到百度实习、商汤经历再到创办MiniMax的创业脉络，系统梳理了多模态路线选择、M系列与H系列产品布局、开源策略（H3发布两周衍生约300个开源模型、fal.ai H3 Max做到3秒生成5秒视频）、API驱动的商业模式，以及他对中美AI生态将走向不同道路的判断。节目还补充了Scottish Mortgage的投资逻辑分析（闫俊杰作为"科学家+资本配置者"的罕见组合）、统一语言+视频模型能让AI从"做片段"转向"做整个项目"的价值，以及价格竞争、亏损等真实挑战。

frontier is the standard by which he judges AGI. rapid post-training to generate five seconds of video in three seconds, turning it into a real-time video generator. Once the speed is up, some brand-new use cases emerge. losses currently about three times the revenue. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 洞察高性價比模型策略：了解 MiniMax 如何在算力資源受限的環境下，以僅十分之一的推論成本實現全球頂尖模型 95% 的效能表現。
  • 拆解多模態與語言模型的整合趨勢：探討將語言與影音生成深度融合為單一模型的技術前瞻性，以及其如何重塑創意與影音製作產業的商業價值。
  • 理解後訓練時代的競爭優勢：藉由精闢的「高爾夫練習球」比喻，掌握為何推論成本是決定強化學習與規模化「後訓練」勝負的核心關鍵。

摘要

從算力狂熱到極致效能的突圍策略

作者指出，MiniMax 創辦人閆俊傑在近期訪談中透露，其模型表現已達到全球頂級模型的 95%，但推論成本僅為十分之一。閆俊傑早年經歷過百度時期最大規模的 GPU 集群研究，深知算力的力量，但在創立 MiniMax 後明確選擇不與美國實驗室硬碰硬比拼硬體規模，而是將核心聚焦於「榨取每顆 GPU 的最大價值」。面對國內外激烈的百模大戰，MiniMax 專注於高勝率的方向，深耕底層系統架構與訓練基礎設施，確保計算晶片能發揮極致運作效率。

以降低成本與科學突破重新定義 AGI

作者提及，MiniMax 的名稱本身就蘊含了「成本最小化、智慧最大化」的願景。閆俊傑對通用人工智慧（AGI）的定義並非僅止於聊天或撰寫文章，而是 AI 能否自主提出全新科學理論以推動人類科學前沿。在技術路徑上，團隊早期便鎖定多模態路線，歷經虛擬陪伴產品 Glow 的驗證與 GPT-4 帶來的時間表震撼，將技術體系收斂為專注生產力的 M 系列語言模型與可跨模態生成的 H 系列影音模型。

打破割裂：邁向全流程統一多模態模型

針對現有影音生成模型的局限，作者引述投資機構觀點指出，當前影音模型雖然畫面出色，卻缺乏理解複雜剪輯指令與創作意圖的能力；而語言模型理解反饋卻無法直接產出畫面。MiniMax 計劃在數月內將 M 系列與 H 系列合併為統一大型模型，這將使 AI 具備承接完整專案、理解細緻修改指令並自動執行的能力，讓未來的商業變現模式從「按秒計費」躍升為「按整體專案交付價值收費」。

低成本推論構築的後訓練飛輪

在商業與營運層面，作者說明 MiniMax 堅持利潤來自技術創新帶來的成本下降，而非調漲價格。針對當前的 AI 競爭格局，訪談中引用了極為生動的「高爾夫練習球比喻」：當今模型能力的躍升關鍵在於消化數據後的「後訓練（Post-training）」，每一次任務嘗試與回饋調整都需要調用推論。如果擁有全球最便宜的練習球（低推論成本），就能以相同預算進行最高頻率的後訓練與強化學習，進而打造出世界上規模最大的後訓練系統，推動模型通往頂級智能。

rapid post-training to generate five seconds of video in three seconds, turning it into a real-time video generator. Once the speed is up, some brand-new use cases emerge. Open-source has another layer of benefits: corporate and government clients can deploy and host models themselves, without needing to send data to MiniMax, making privacy and. security easier to control. Over the past six months, the issue of AI sovereignty has become increasingly critical. If your business is built on a centralized model, can you really count on continued access in the long run? What exactly will happen to your data? These concerns have given open-source models a natural advantage. Yan Yunjie says that open source is not the opposite of commercialization, but a catalyst for it and for continuous innovation; it’s a triple win for model vendors, end users, and developers. The plan is to remain committed to open source until AGI is achieved. The core goal is to deliver 95%of the performance at 1%of the cost. Yan Yunjie cautions. that what truly matters is not the gap at a specific point in time, but the speed of model iteration, as both China and the U.S. are still in the very early stages on the road to AGI. He notes that this final 5%gap may be even harder to bridge than the initial 95%progress. So , closing the current gap may take more time; over the past three years, the pace of progress between U.S. and Chinese models has been roughly comparable, and he focuses on iteration rates rather than leaderboard rankings. Regarding the issue of compute constraints, he says this is something Chinese AI companies must face together , but it is precisely these constraints that have made them better engineers and. researchers. The more limited the compute, the more critical algorithmic innovation and inference optimization become. Many cutting-edge U.S. labs are somewhat spoiled by an abundance of compute, allowing them to explore the boundaries of model capabilities at scale without being forced to prioritize efficiency from day one like Chinese companies. Yan also says he designed the model architecture with the intent that it could maintain excellent performance regardless of the chip it runs on. When hardware is constrained, the value of model architecture, infrastructure, and low-level optimization is amplified many times over. Regarding the differences.

between the U.S. and Chinese AI ecosystems, Yan’s judgment is clear: they will not follow the same path. The U.S. ecosystem is using massive capital to support closed systems, while the Chinese ecosystem is using efficiency to support collaboration. U.S. companies have more compute, more funding, and easier access to chips, while Chinese companies are forced to maximize output efficiency per unit of compute. Open source versus closed, high efficiency versus resource abundance—these fundamental differences will breed different types of innovation. Why invest in 01.AI? Second is Yan Junjie himself; Burns says he rarely meets someone who is both a highly respected AI scientist and an excellent capital allocator. AI labs, especially those in the U.S., will pour massive amounts of money into running dozens of experimental paths at once to see which. one succeeds. Burns said he spoke with many in the Chinese AI circle who have worked with Yan for years, and everyone agrees his ability to predict tech trends is a core strength, while his reputation as a scientist helps him attract top-tier AI talent. losses currently about three times the revenue. Regarding organizational culture, Yan Junjie summarizes MiniMax's principles into two points: first, keep things simple; although there are multi-modal models, the underlying architecture and infrastructure remain very streamlined. Second, always build infrastructure. Refining infrastructure is sometimes more important than launching products quickly, as it is the foundation for scaling. Other traits, such as a flat. structure, efficiency, and focus, are simply the results of these two principles naturally evolving under constraints. Finally, when asked what the world will look like after MiniMax achieves its vision, Yan Junjie said the question isn't whether AI can achieve it , but who it will benefit. AI is so important that it shouldn't belong to any one company, country, or organization; it must belong to all of humanity. He said the company's mission statement is "Intelligence with everyone ," rather than "Intelligence for everyone," as if intelligence were something they provide to everyone. In. his view, AGI should belong to the model's users, the developers building applications on top of it, and the researchers contributing to it; together , they determine what kind of system the model ultimately becomes. Watching this interview, my biggest takeaway is that Yan Jing has shown us an AI expansion path that is completely different from the mainstream Silicon Valley model. The Silicon Valley story is about more compute, more money, and training larger models, while Max's story is about doing more efficient things with fewer resources. It is hard to say who will succeed on. this path, but one thing is certain: the global AI race is not just playing out in Silicon Valley.
